metadata.title: The role of parental involvement in adolescents’ digital reading performance

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 reading data with a hierarchical structure (students nested within schools, nested within countries). The authors restricted the sample to countries that administered both the student and parent questionnaires, then used the resulting linked student–parent records for analysis. They normalized the student weight W_FSTUWT to promote unbiased estimates, consistent with OECD guidance for PISA analyses. The paper does not report replicate-weight procedures (e.g., BRR/jackknife), but it does implement a three-level HLM to account for clustering across country and school levels.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Data were extracted from the PISA 2018 reading-themed cycle and linked with the parent questionnaire; the analysis was restricted to countries that voluntarily administered both the student questionnaire and the parent questionnaire. The analytic sample includes all 15-year-old students, with exclusions for special education needs and language differences. For variables used in the parental-involvement constructs, the authors assessed missingness and excluded EXPECTAP_4 from the analysis due to higher missingness, while applying multiple imputation to handle remaining missing values (with MI datasets matched to the corresponding plausible values).

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Reading (digital reading performance; age 15; 12 countries)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Three-level HLM with PVs (10 PVs analyzed separately and combined via Rubin’s rules). Fixed-effect estimates: PRESUPP β=0.021 (SE=0.004, p<0.001); CURSUPP β=-0.041 (SE=0.003, p<0.001); PASCHPOL β=-0.047 (SE=0.003, p<0.001); EMOSUPP β=0.055 (SE=0.003, p<0.001); JOYREADP β=0.060 (SE=0.003, p<0.001). Interaction: PREEMO (PRECUPP×EMOSUPP) positive (reported as only significant positive interaction). Random-effect variance: student-level f2=8.429%, school-level f2=49.630%, country-level f2=86.076%.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Reading data (digital reading performance; age 15; 12 countries), the study leveraged previous parental support, current parental support, school policies for parental involvement, parental emotional support, and parental enjoyment of reading to predict digital reading performance (PVs 1–10 averaged), finding that emotional involvement (EMOSUPP, JOYREADP) and previous behavioral support (PRESUPP) were positively associated, while current behavioral support (CURSUPP) and school policies for behavioral involvement (PASCHPOL) were negatively associated. This indicates that strengthening emotionally supportive and sustained reading-related parental engagement may be more beneficial for adolescents’ digital reading outcomes than increasing short-term or school-policy-driven involvement, though the study is correlational and cannot establish causality.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2018 reading (digital reading performance) for 15-year-olds in 12 countries (N=83,043; 3,342 schools), linking student and parent questionnaire responses. Outcomes are the 10 PISA plausible values for reading, handled by running separate analyses for each PV and combining results using Rubin’s rules; missing data were addressed with multiple imputation after excluding EXPECTAP_4. The authors fit a three-level HLM (country–school–student) with W_FSTUWT normalized, and report fixed effects and effect sizes (f2) at student, school, and country levels. Key results show positive associations for previous parental support in reading-related activities (β=0.021) and emotional involvement (EMOSUPP β=0.055; JOYREADP β=0.060), while current parental support (β=-0.041) and school policies for parental behavioral involvement (β=-0.047) are negative. The paper emphasizes correlations rather than causal effects, and relies on parent-reported measures that may be influenced by social desirability.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This extraction treats the paper as an exploratory correlational multilevel analysis rather than an ML predictive-modeling study: the methodology uses three-level HLM with PVs and multiple imputation, and the results report regression-style coefficients rather than training/evaluating machine-learning algorithms. Consequently, ml_techniques are left empty because no ML learners (e.g., Random Forest, XGBoost, SVM) are reported as being trained or compared.
